cell.label: History and physical examination: scarring present or absent?
Hereditary disorders; trauma: mechanical, burns, caustic agents, radiation; or systemic disease: discoid lupus, sarcoidosis, lichen planus, necrobiosis lipoidica, others
Infection (fungal, bacterial, protozoan); or neoplasm: basal cell carcinoma (morpheaform), squamous cell carcinoma, metastatic carcinoma (alopecia neoplastica), lymphoma, or adnexal tumors
Total testosterone, free testosterone, DHEA-S, prolactin levels
Thyroid function tests to rule out thyroid disease VDRL test to rule out syphilis Ferritin level to rule out iron deficiency ANA test to rule out systemic lupus erythematosus

Laboratory results normal; consider: other nutritional deficiency (malnutrition, sprue, zinc deficiency) Telogen effluvium Trauma (trichotillomania, traction alopecia) Hereditary syndromes Alopecia areata Androgenetic alopecia

footnotes.footnote: *Clinical signs and symptoms of androgen excess include menstrual irregularities, infertility, hirsutism, severe cystic acne, virilization, and galactorrhea. Abbreviations:DHEA-S, dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate; VDRL, Venereal Disease Research Laboratory; ANA, antinuclear antibody.

Adapted from Healey PM, Jacobson EJ. Common Medical Diagnoses: An Algorithmic Approach. 3rd, Philadelphia: W.B. Saunders, 2000; 208-211, with additional information from Drake LA, Dinehart SM, Farmer ER, et al. Guidelines of care for androgenetic alopecia. American Academy of Dermatology.
